segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Suddenly a sound came from heaven like the rush of a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And there appeared to them tongues as of fire, divided among them, and one settled on each of them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them to speak out.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there were Jews living in Jerusalem, devout men from every nation under heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At this sound the crowd gathered and was thrown into confusion, because each one heard them speaking in his own language.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were astounded and amazed, and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, aren’t all these who are speaking Galileans?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So how is it that each of us hears them in our own language, the one we were born into?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Parthians and Medes and Elamites, and those who live in Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene, and visitors from Rome,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: both Jews and converts, Cretans and Arabs—we hear them speaking in our own tongues of the great deeds of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were all astounded and at a loss, saying to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What does this mean?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But others mocked and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “They are full of sweet wine.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter, standing with the eleven, raised his voice and spoke out to them:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Fellow Jews and all you who live in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: These people are not drunk, as you suppose, for it is only the third hour of the day.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: No, this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: ‘And it will be in the last days, God says, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy, and your young men will see visions, and your old men will dream dreams.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Yes, even on my slaves, men and women alike, I will pour out my Spirit in those days, and they will prophesy.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And I will give wonders in the sky above and signs on the earth below, blood and fire and a cloud of smoke.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the day of the Lord comes, the great and glorious day.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And it will be that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Fellow Israelites, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with deeds of power and wonders and signs that God did through him among you, as you yourselves know—

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: this man, handed over by the fixed plan and foreknowledge of God, you nailed up and killed by the hands of lawless men.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But God raised him up, bringing the pangs of death to an end, because it was not possible for him to be held by it.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For David says of him: ‘I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand so that I may not be shaken.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Therefore my heart was glad and my tongue rejoiced, and my flesh too will dwell in hope,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: because you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you let your faithful one see decay.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You have made known to me the paths of life; you will fill me with gladness in your presence.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Brothers, I may speak to you plainly about the patriarch David: he both died and was buried, and his tomb is among us to this day.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So, being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath to seat one from the fruit of his loins on his throne,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Messiah, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see decay.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: This Jesus God raised up, and of that we are all witnesses.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Exalted, then, to the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you see and hear.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For David did not go up into the heavens, but he himself says: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So let the whole house of Israel know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Messiah, this Jesus whom you crucified.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard this they were cut to the heart, and they said to Peter and the rest of the apostles,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brothers, what should we do?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Turn back, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far away, as many as the Lord our God calls to himself.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: With many other words he bore solemn witness and kept urging them, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Be saved from this crooked generation.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So those who welcomed his word were baptized, and about three thousand people were added that day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were devoted to the apostles’ teaching and to the common life, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Awe came over everyone, and many wonders and signs were taking place through the apostles.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All who believed were together and held everything in common,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they would sell their property and possessions and divide the proceeds among all, as anyone had need.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Day by day they were devoted, with one mind, to being in the temple; and breaking bread in their homes, they shared their food with great joy and simplicity of heart,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: praising God and having favor with all the people. And day by day the Lord added to their company those who were being saved.

notes.note: The word means 'fiftieth' and was the Greek name for the Jewish Feast of Weeks, the harvest festival held on the fiftieth day after Passover. It was one of the three pilgrimage festivals, which helps explain why Jerusalem was so full of Jews from abroad.

The Greek word means both the tongue as an organ and a language. Verses 6–11 show that real foreign languages, understood by their native speakers, are meant here. 'Tongues' is kept so that the echo of the 'tongues as of fire' in verse 3 is not lost. A minority of scholars think Luke has reshaped an account of ecstatic speech.

The Greek word here is the same one that in the plural is usually translated 'Gentiles', meaning the non-Jewish peoples. Here it plainly means the nations of the world as ethnic and political units, among whom these Jews had been living.
This is the Roman province of Asia, the western part of modern Turkey with Ephesus as its chief city, and not the continent.

The Greek is literally 'Men, Jews', a formal style of address also seen in verses 22 and 29. Many translations render it 'Men of Judea', taking the word geographically alongside 'all who live in Jerusalem'. Since verse 5 uses the same word for Jews from every nation now living in the city, the ethnic sense is preferred here, but either is possible.

notes.phrase: the third hour of the day
notes.traditional: the third hour of the day
notes.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour is about nine in the morning. Peter's point is that it is far too early in the day for anyone to be drunk.

notes.phrase: my slaves, men and women alike
notes.traditional: my servants, both men and women (or 'menservants and maidservants')
notes.note: The Greek words are the ordinary masculine and feminine terms for slaves, and a first-century reader would have heard them that way. Most translations soften this to 'servants'. In Joel the line extends the gift of the Spirit down to the lowest social rank; the added 'my' in Acts makes them God's own slaves.

The word can mean 'wicked' in general or, more specifically, 'those without the Law', that is, Gentiles. Many scholars think the second sense is intended here, pointing to the Romans who carried out the execution. The rendering leaves both possibilities open.

notes.traditional: the pains of death / the agony of death
notes.note: The Greek word normally means the pains of childbirth. The phrase comes from the Greek version of the Psalms (for example Psalm 18:4–5), where it translates a Hebrew word that can mean either 'cords' or 'pangs'. Whether Luke intends an image of death in labour, unable to hold back what it must give up, is debated.

This is not the usual Greek word for 'holy' but one meaning devout or loyal to God, used in the Greek Psalms for the Hebrew word for a faithful worshipper. Most translations have 'your Holy One', often capitalised as a title. The rendering here keeps the two Greek words distinct; the quotation is from Psalm 16:8–11.

The Greek word means 'anointed one' and here, as in verse 36, it is a title for Israel's expected king, which 'Messiah' conveys more directly than 'Christ'. Where it is attached to Jesus's name, as in verse 38, 'Christ' is kept. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

notes.phrase: to the right hand of God
notes.traditional: exalted to (or at) the right hand of God
notes.note: The Greek can equally mean 'exalted by the right hand of God', that is, by God's power. 'To the right hand' is chosen because the psalm quoted in the next verse speaks of sitting at God's right hand, but the other reading has scholarly support.

'Repent' now suggests mainly feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term that readers understand to include a changed life.

The Greek word means sharing or partnership and is related to the word 'common' in verse 44. 'Fellowship' is the usual rendering, but in modern usage it often suggests little more than social time. Scholars disagree whether the word here refers to the community's bond in general or specifically to the sharing of goods described in the following verses.

Later manuscripts read 'added to the church', which is the source of the King James wording. The earliest manuscripts lack 'the church' and have only a phrase meaning 'together' or 'to the same group', the same expression used in verses 1 and 44.

candidates.reason: Translations vary between 'slave', 'servant' and 'bondservant' across the Gospels, Acts and the letters, and the choice changes how readers hear both social references and the metaphor of belonging to God or Christ.
The word ranges over 'soul', 'life', 'self' and 'person' throughout the New Testament, and inconsistent handling will mislead readers about what is being said of the human person.
Rendered variously as 'fellowship', 'sharing', 'participation', 'communion' and 'partnership' in Acts and the letters; one policy by sense is needed.
Whether to say 'tongues' or 'languages' must be settled consistently between Acts 2, 10 and 19 and 1 Corinthians 12–14, since the choice shapes how readers understand the phenomenon.
In the plural, of Jesus's and the apostles' acts, it is rendered 'miracles', 'mighty works' or 'deeds of power', and should be uniform across the Gospels, Acts and the letters.
